consumer_seed: The Ofcom contracts page was published on 21 September 2015.
The Ofcom contracts page was last updated on 26 June 2026.
The monthly amount payable during a contract should be provided clearly before sign-up.
If a provider raises prices beyond what was agreed, it must give at least one month's notice and a penalty-free exit right.
Scheduled in-contract price increases should be made clear at the point of sale.
Providers must clearly state post-rise prices in pounds and pence and when the rises will occur.
Businesses are entitled to request specified contract information in a clear, comprehensible and easily accessible form.
Requested contract information can include whether services may be limited or restricted.
Requested contract information can include minimum service-quality levels such as ongoing quality and initial connection time.
Requested contract information can include the customer-service and maintenance service supplied with the contract.
Requested contract information can include contract length and renewal conditions.
Requested contract information can include termination charges, including early termination charges.
A small business with ten employees or fewer must receive key contract information before sign-up.
The pre-contract summary should be one page, or three pages for bundled services.
The contract summary should include charges, contract length and the cancellation process.
Customers with disabilities can request contract information in reasonably acceptable formats such as large print or Braille.
A provider must obtain consent before renewing a new minimum term for a small business with ten employees or fewer using landline or broadband services.
For a small business with ten employees or fewer, the contract length should not exceed 24 months.
After a mobile Auto-Switch, the former provider must not charge for a notice period running beyond the switch date.
A business service-level agreement can define support and problem-resolution terms, including repair, installation, coverage and connection measures.
The Ofcom provider-choice page was published on 12 April 2017.
The Ofcom provider-choice page was last updated on 10 February 2026.
Mobile signal strength varies by place and provider.
Mobile signal can be affected by mast distance and buildings or natural obstacles.
Ofcom recommends Map Your Mobile to check likely signal where people live and work.
Mobile price can depend on provider, allowance, features, contract length and whether a handset is included.
Ofcom-accredited comparison services must be transparent, accessible, accurate, comprehensive and up to date.
Broadband, phone and pay-TV customers must receive best-deal information when the initial contract ends and annually while out of contract.
Experienced broadband speed can vary with time of day, connected people and devices, and Wi-Fi versus wired use.
Providers signed to the broadband speed codes provide a speed estimate online and at the point of sale.
The Ofcom telecoms complaints report was published on 25 January 2024.
The Ofcom telecoms complaints report was last updated on 30 July 2026.
Ofcom receives complaints about landline, fixed broadband, pay-monthly mobile and pay-TV services.
Provider complaint comparisons are published quarterly relative to customer-base size, per 100,000 customers.
In Q1 2026 fixed-broadband and pay-monthly-mobile complaints decreased, while landline and pay-TV complaints stayed the same versus Q4 2025.
Plusnet and TalkTalk generated the most landline complaints in Q1 2026.
EE, Sky, Utility Warehouse, Virgin Media and Vodafone were the least complained-about landline providers in Q1 2026.
Sky Mobile was the most complained-about pay-monthly mobile provider in Q1 2026, mainly driven by switching experiences.
EE, Giffgaff, Tesco Mobile, Three and Vodafone generated the least pay-monthly-mobile complaints in Q1 2026.
EE and Virgin Media were the most complained-about pay-TV providers in Q1 2026, with different leading complaint drivers.
The Ofcom train-connectivity research news release was published on 3 June 2026.
Mobile performance was poor in between 58% and 83% of train tests, depending on the network.
The research measured 24 railway-line segments across England, Scotland and Wales.
Good performance was defined as at least 5 Mbit/s download, 1.5 Mbit/s upload and 50 milliseconds or less response time.
EE met the good-performance standard on 42% of measured railway segments.
Three met the good-performance standard on 21% of measured railway segments.
O2 met the good-performance standard on 20% of measured railway segments.
Vodafone met the good-performance standard on 17% of measured railway segments.
On-board train Wi-Fi performed well in only 1% of the measured tests.
Ofcom reported £10 billion of UK mobile-network investment since 2020 and a 20% real-terms fall in average-user prices.
